title: What We Keep

post.author: u/night_files_vasanthi
post.title: I'm the night researcher at a small private-investigation agency. A former client asked what we hold about her. Tonight I found two weeks of her neighbours' evenings, written down in 2016.

blocks.text: I'm Vasanthi, night researcher at Fenwhistle Enquiries, a private-investigation agency of four people in Singapore. By day our investigators watch and ask. At night I search our files and type up their notes.

Mr Thiruchelvam founded it in 2014, and keeps everything, in case. We've opened 214 cases since. Each case leaves ten records of four kinds: the client's contact details, five case notes, two notes on other people the case touched, and two invoices, the bills we sent. That makes 2,140 records, 2014 to 2026. We have no written rule on how long any of them stays. Nobody has ever deleted one.

Anything that can identify a living person is called personal data: a name, a phone number, a note of when someone leaves home. Nearly every record we hold is personal data, about clients and people who never hired us.

In many places a person can ask a business for a copy of the personal data it holds on them. That is an access request. Singapore's law on it is the PDPA, short for Personal Data Protection Act. The regulator's guidance says an organisation it covers must answer as soon as reasonably possible. If it can't within 30 days, it must write and say when it will.
Answering one goes in four steps. Check the person is who they say. Search every file for them. Take out anything about other people. Send the rest.

Ms Brannigan's request came by email on Monday 21 September. She hired us once, in November 2016. Mr Thiruchelvam checked her identity, then left the request in his tray. The 30 days end on Wednesday 21 October. Tonight, Tuesday 13 October, he asked me to put her reply together.

At 22:10 I searched the shared drive, the office computer's store of all our files, for her name. One folder came back: her 2016 case, ten records. Six of its lines follow. Each shows a record's date, its kind, and what it holds, in general words:

07 Nov 2016  contact  her name, address and phone
07 Nov 2016  case     what she asked us to find
07-20 Nov    other    a couple across the road: times out and back, visitors
07-20 Nov    other    the man next door: times out and back, his car
02 Dec 2016  case     case closed; file kept, no reason recorded
02 Dec 2016  invoice  final

Someone kept scratching her car outside her flat. Our investigator watched her street from Monday 7 to Sunday 20 November 2016 and wrote down who came and went. The case closed on Friday 2 December 2016. The notes on her neighbours stayed: three people who never hired us and never knew.
Two weeks of a stranger's evenings, kept almost ten years for no reason anyone can name.

blocks.label: shared_drive_13_october.png

diagram.aria: My sketch of where our records live on 13 October 2026. Top row: the shared drive, holding 2,140 records from 2014 to 2026, copied every night at 02:00 to an online backup store, where no copy has been deleted since 2014. Bottom row: the four kinds of record on the drive: 214 contact details, 1,070 case notes, 428 notes on other people who were never clients, and 428 invoices. A note says her 2016 file is 10 of these records.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from my sketch on 13 October 2026. 214 cases since 2014, ten records each: 214 contact details, 1,070 case notes, 428 notes on people who were never clients, 428 invoices. Every night at 02:00 the whole drive is copied to the online store, and no copy has ever been deleted. Her 2016 file is 10 of the 2,140 records.

blocks.text: The notes aren't only in that folder. Every night at 02:00 the office computer copies the whole drive to a rented online store. Each copy is a backup: a spare to restore from, or copy back, after a mistake. Every nightly copy since 2014 is still there.
Nothing is scrambled, either. Scrambling data with a key, so only the key's holder can read it, is encryption. Ours has none.
I haven't sent the reply. Mr Thiruchelvam says our files are what make us good. What should we change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Three questions before you choose, Vasanthi. What was each note on a neighbour written for? People who handle personal data call that reason its purpose. Is the purpose still being served today? If you deleted the folder tonight, how long would it live on in the backups? And the three people in those notes, the ones who aren't asking, are called third parties: what did any of them agree to?

replies.author: u/night_files_vasanthi
replies.text: For the car case, and it closed on 2 December 2016. Nothing on file says why anything was kept after. The backup store keeps every nightly copy, so a deleted folder would stay there for good. And the neighbours agreed to nothing. They never knew.

comments.author: u/keep_it_all_lindgard
comments.text: Don't delete a thing. In this line of work you never know which old note will crack a case. A face from 2016 turns up in a new job, and that note is your only proof. Encrypt the lot so no outsider can ever read it, take the neighbours out of her copy, and keep the files. A shredder can't give anything back.

replies.author: u/night_files_vasanthi
replies.text: Mr Thiruchelvam read this over my shoulder and nodded at every line.

comments.author: u/sign_here_rowntree
comments.text: Or get it in writing. Have every client sign a form saying the agency may keep their file forever. Agreement given freely is what data protection laws call consent, and with it on file nobody can say you kept anything without asking.

reply.prompt: Ms Brannigan's reply is due by Wednesday 21 October. What should Fenwhistle change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Encrypt every old case file, so even data kept since 2016 is safe from any outsider.
options.part2: Mr Thiruchelvam paid for encryption on the shared drive and the backup store. We replayed the six weeks in the sim with encryption on and nothing else changed. A stolen disk or backup copy now shows nothing readable. But her reply is built inside the office, by people who hold the key, so it still held 10 records and named 3 people who were never clients. I took the neighbours' notes out by hand before it went out on Tuesday 20 October. On Monday 26 October nothing was deleted: 2,140 records stayed, 428 of them notes on people who never hired us, her neighbours' among them, and every nightly copy since 2014 stayed too. A week later one of those neighbours, who had heard she'd asked, sent an access request of his own. The honest answer was two weeks of his evenings in 2016.
options.senior: Encryption protects data from people who don't hold the key; it does nothing about whether you should hold the data at all. Singapore's regulator says personal data that is archived or locked away is still retained, and the agency itself reads it with the key, so every access request, every leak by an insider and every misuse still reaches it. Encrypt what you keep, yes, but first keep only what has a purpose, for as long as the purpose lasts.

options.text: Remove the neighbours' notes before sending, so she sees only what is about herself.
options.part2: I took the two notes on her neighbours out of her copy, as the regulator's guidance asks: personal data about other people is masked or left out of an access reply. In the sim, with other people taken out, her reply on Tuesday 20 October held 8 records, all hers, and named 0 people who were never clients. She was satisfied. But nothing else changed: on Monday 26 October all 2,140 records were still on the drive, 428 of them notes on people who never hired us, including the two about her street, and every nightly copy since 2014 still held them. A week later one of her neighbours, who had heard she'd asked, sent an access request of his own. The honest answer was two weeks of his evenings in 2016.
options.senior: Taking third parties out of an access reply is required under the PDPA, if it covers your organisation, and under GDPR, the EU's data protection law, if it applies to you, so do it every time. But it is a step in answering one request, not a design. The notes still sit on the drive and in every backup with no purpose, and the next request, a leak or a court order finds them. The fix that ends the problem is deciding how long each kind of record lives and deleting it on time.

options.text: Ask every client to sign a form agreeing that the agency may keep their file forever.
options.part2: Mr Thiruchelvam had a form drawn up, and every new client from November signed it. A signed form is not a setting in the sim, because it changes no number: on Tuesday 20 October her reply still held 10 records and named 3 people who were never clients, and on Monday 26 October all 2,140 records stayed, 428 of them notes on people who never hired us. The three people on her street signed nothing. Their notes were collected for a car case that closed in 2016, and a client's signature can't agree for them. A week later one of those neighbours sent an access request of his own. The honest answer was two weeks of his evenings in 2016.
options.senior: Consent covers the person who gives it, for the purposes they were told about. It can't stand in for third parties, and "keep it forever" is not a purpose. Singapore's regulator says personal data must not be kept "just in case" for purposes the person wasn't told about. Ask what each record is for, and keep it only as long as that purpose, or a legal duty, needs it.

options.text: Set how long each kind of record is kept and why, then delete it, backups too.
options.part2: Mr Thiruchelvam let me write the rule he never had. Each record now carries a purpose label: its kind and the case it serves. The schedule, as given data: contact details, case notes and invoices kept 7 years after the year the case closed, which covers the tax office's 5 years and a contract claim; notes on people who never hired us, until the end of the year after the case closed. Each nightly backup copy is now kept 35 days, then deleted. On Tuesday 20 October, a day early, Ms Brannigan got her reply: 8 records, her own, with the two notes on her neighbours taken out, and a line saying her file would now be deleted. In the sim, the first deletion run on Monday 26 October removed 950 records; 1,190 remain, 70 of them notes on people who never hired us, all from 2025 and 2026 cases. Her 2016 file left the drive that day and the last backup on Monday 30 November, 35 days on. The schedule waits whenever a request is open.
options.senior: Privacy is mostly decided by what you keep. Give every kind of personal data a purpose and a keep period with its reason written down, label each record so the deletion job can tell the kinds apart, and delete on schedule, pausing only for an open request or a legal duty. Make deletion reach the backups by keeping them on a fixed cycle, so a deleted record is gone everywhere by a date you can name. Then encrypt what remains and take third parties out of every access reply. Kept for a reason, gone on time: that is what the PDPA's retention rule and GDPR's storage limitation both ask.

sim.title: Play Fenwhistle's six weeks, and choose what it keeps
sim.lede: You're Vasanthi, on Tuesday 13 October 2026, before the 22:10 search. As given data: Fenwhistle opened 214 cases from 2014 to 2026 (12, 14, 16, 15, 17, 18, 14, 16, 18, 19, 20, 20 and 15 a year), and every case leaves 10 records: 1 contact record, 5 case notes, 2 notes on other people the case touched, people who never hired the agency, and 2 invoices. That is 2,140 records. Ms Brannigan's 2016 file is 10 of them; its 2 notes on other people name 3 neighbours. Her request came on Monday 21 September, the 30 days end on Wednesday 21 October, and the reply goes out on Tuesday 20 October. The schedule, also given data: contact details, case notes and invoices kept 7 years after the year the case closed, notes on other people 1 year; the first deletion run is Monday 26 October; with deletion reaching backups, each nightly copy is kept 35 days. Choose how long records are kept (everything, as built, or a schedule per kind), whether each record carries a purpose label, a tag saying its kind and the case it serves, whether deletion reaches the backups, whether other people's data is taken out of access replies, and whether the drive and backups are encrypted. Then play to 30 November and read the records held by year and kind, her reply line by line, the people in it who were never clients, and when her 2016 file leaves the drive and the last backup.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play it as built. Her reply holds 10 records and names 3 people who were never clients, and all 2,140 records stay. Turn encryption on: a stolen copy shows nothing readable, and the reply and the 2,140 stay the same. Turn encryption off and take other people out of replies: 8 records, 0 strangers, still 2,140 held. Switch to a schedule: 1,400 held, 280 notes on others, and the backups never let go. Add purpose labels: 950 removed, 1,190 held, 70 notes on others. Let deletion reach the backups: her 2016 file leaves the drive on 26 October and the last backup on 30 November 2026, 35 days on.

explain.oneLine: Nobody broke in. An agency kept every record "in case", so an ordinary access request turned up three strangers' evenings from 2016, kept for no purpose on the drive and in every backup. Give each kind of record a purpose and a keep period, delete on time, let the backups age out on a fixed cycle, and take third parties out of every reply.

steps.title: Personal data comes with a reason.
steps.text: Personal data is anything that identifies a living person, and the law in many places ties it to a purpose: the reason it was collected. The neighbour notes had one, the car case, and it ended on 2 December 2016. Purpose limitation says data collected for one reason is used for that reason. Minimisation says collect only what the purpose needs: the investigator needed to know when the scratches happened, which may never have needed the names of three households. If GDPR applies to you, its Article 5 states both.

steps.title: A retention schedule: how long, and why.
steps.text: A retention schedule is a list of every kind of record, how long each is kept, and the reason. First, list the kinds: contact details, case notes, notes on other people, invoices. Second, give each a keep period and write down why: the tax office's 5 years for invoices, a contract claim for case notes, nothing after the case for notes on people who were never clients. Third, label every record with its kind and its case, so a program can tell them apart. Fourth, run the deletion on a fixed day. What goes wrong: without labels the job can only apply the longest period to everything, 1,400 records instead of 1,190; and a schedule nobody runs is a document, not a deletion.

steps.title: Deletion has to reach the backups.
steps.text: Deleting a file from the drive leaves every backup that already holds it. First, decide how long each backup copy lives, here 35 days. Second, delete each copy when it reaches that age. Then anything deleted from the live data is gone from the last copy 35 days later: her 2016 file, deleted on Monday 26 October, is gone on Monday 30 November. What goes wrong: backups kept forever never let go, and restoring an old copy brings deleted records back, so keep a list of what was deleted, by record id and not by contents, and run it again after any restore.

steps.title: Answering an access request.
steps.text: First, check the person is who they say. Second, search every store you control for them. Third, hold those records back from deletion while you answer. Fourth, take out other people's personal data, by masking or leaving it out. Fifth, send it within the time allowed: if the PDPA covers you, the guidance of the PDPC, Singapore's Personal Data Protection Commission, says as soon as reasonably possible, and if you can't within 30 days, tell the person in writing when you will; if GDPR applies, within one month, which may be extended by two further months for complex requests. What goes wrong: a search that misses a store, a reply that hands over a neighbour's evenings, and a deadline lost in someone's tray.

steps.title: Why encryption and a consent form don't fix it.
steps.text: Encryption keeps outsiders out, and the PDPC says data that is archived or locked away is still retained: the agency holds the key, so every request and every insider still reaches it. A client's signature covers that client, for the purposes she was told about, never her neighbours, and "forever" is not a purpose. Both are worth having for what they do. Neither decides what to keep.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for Ms Brannigan's 2016 file. Her file's 10 records each carry a label saying their kind. The retention schedule keeps contact details, case notes and invoices 7 years after the case year and notes on others 1 year, and says when the deletion run happens: Monday 26 October 2026. The run deletes the file from live data that day. The nightly backups, each kept 35 days, let go of it by Monday 30 November 2026.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for Ms Brannigan's 2016 file. Each record's label tells the schedule its kind; the schedule says when it goes. The run on Monday 26 October deletes the file from live data, and because each nightly backup is kept 35 days, the last copy holding it is gone on Monday 30 November 2026.

fix.title: The fix: a purpose and a keep period for every kind of record, deletion that reaches the backups
fix.text: Write down every kind of personal data the agency keeps, what each is for, how long it is kept and why: contact details, case notes and invoices 7 years after the case year, covering the tax office's records rule and a contract claim; notes on people who never hired the agency, only until the end of the year after the case closes. Label every record with its kind and its case. Run the deletion on a fixed day, the first on Monday 26 October 2026, which removes 950 of the 2,140 records and leaves 1,190. Keep each nightly backup 35 days and then delete it, so anything deleted is gone from every copy by a date you can name: Monday 30 November for her 2016 file. Pause deletion for any record an open request or legal duty covers. Keep a list of deleted record ids and run it again after any restore. For every access reply, search every store, take third parties out, and answer within the time allowed. Then encrypt what remains, and collect less to start with: write down what a case needs before the watching starts.

limits: A backup cycle sets a delay, not an instant. For 35 days after a deletion, the record still sits in older copies, and restoring one of them brings it back unless the deletion list is run again.

A schedule is only as good as its labels and its reasons. A record with no kind, or one copied into an email or onto a laptop, sits outside the job, and a keep period nobody can explain will not survive a regulator's question.

Keep periods are judgements, not rules from this case. Tax, contract and sector rules differ by country and change; the 7 years here are given data, so check your own legal duties with someone qualified.

explain.seniorTake: In a privacy incident the frightening record is often not a stolen one. It is one you kept, for no reason anyone can name, until someone asked. Every kind of personal data needs a purpose, a keep period with its reason written down, and a day it is deleted, and the design has to make that deletion real: labels so a program can tell kinds apart, a job that runs on a fixed day and pauses for open requests, and backups on a fixed cycle so deleted data leaves the last copy by a date you can name. Collect less in the first place, because data you never wrote down needs no schedule. Encryption and consent are both worth having, but neither answers the question of what to keep: encryption protects the data from outsiders, not from your own access replies, and a client's signature never covers the people in her file. Answer access requests as a process: verify, search every store, hold, take third parties out, send on time. The PDPA's retention rule and GDPR's storage limitation ask the same thing in different words: keep it for a reason, and let it go when the reason ends.

realWorld.title: PDPA: stop keeping it once the purpose ends
realWorld.text: Singapore's regulator, the PDPC, summarises section 25: it "requires an organisation to cease to retain its documents containing personal data, or remove the means by which the personal data can be associated with particular individuals, as soon as it is reasonable to assume that the purpose for which that personal data was collected is no longer being served by retention of the personal data, and retention is no longer necessary for legal or business purposes." If your organisation is covered by the PDPA, that is the rule the neighbour notes broke.

realWorld.title: PDPC: not 'just in case', and archived still counts
realWorld.text: The same guidance says "personal data must not be kept by an organisation 'just in case' it may be needed for other purposes that have not been notified to the individual concerned." And it closes the encryption loophole: "Like physical documents, personal data in electronic form(s) which are archived or to which access is limited will still be considered to be retained for the purposes of the Retention Limitation Obligation."

realWorld.title: PDPC: a retention policy, kind by kind
realWorld.text: The guidance says an organisation "may have to implement varying retention periods for each type of personal data as appropriate", and "As good practice, organisations should prepare an appropriate personal data retention policy which sets out their approach to retention periods for personal data." For contracts, it gives an example: actions must be brought within 6 years, so "an organisation may wish to retain records relating to its contracts for 7 years from the date of termination of the contract".

realWorld.title: PDPC: 30 days, and other people masked
realWorld.text: On timing: "If an organisation is unable to respond to an access request within 30 days after receiving the request, the organisation shall inform the individual in writing within 30 days of the time by which it will be able to respond to the request." On other people in the file, it suggests "masking out the personal data of other individual(s) before providing the personal data requested by the individual."

realWorld.title: PDPC: hold it while you answer, but not forever
realWorld.text: Where data is deleted on a schedule, the organisation is to "ensure the personal data requested is preserved while the organisation is processing the access request." But it adds that organisations "should not retain personal data indefinitely when there is no business or legal purpose to do so." That is why Fenwhistle's schedule waits for an open request, then runs.

realWorld.title: GDPR Article 5: purpose, minimisation, storage
realWorld.text: If GDPR applies to you, Article 5 says personal data shall be "collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes", "adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed" (data minimisation), and "kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed" (storage limitation).

realWorld.title: GDPR Article 15: a copy, without harming others
realWorld.text: Article 15(3): "The controller shall provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing." Article 15(4): "The right to obtain a copy referred to in paragraph 3 shall not adversely affect the rights and freedoms of others." That second line is the neighbours.

realWorld.title: GDPR Article 12: within one month
realWorld.text: Article 12(3) asks for an answer "without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt of the request." It adds: "That period may be extended by two further months where necessary, taking into account the complexity and number of the requests."

realWorld.title: A retention fine: O2 Advertising, Singapore, 2019
realWorld.text: The PDPC's decision says an advertising firm collected people's data in 2015 for a client's campaign. It "admitted that it had overlooked deleting the Disclosed Data and that there were no reasonable grounds to continue retaining them after the engagement with its client ceased in 2016." The data was found exposed online, and "was only deleted by the Organisation after it was informed by the Commission of the complaint." The firm was found in breach of section 25, along with the protection and accountability obligations. Its status: the decision itself records that, after the firm's representations about its finances, "the Commissioner has decided to reduce the financial penalty to $10,000", a figure that "should not be taken as setting any precedent for future cases." The decision page we read notes no later appeal.

realWorld.title: Invoices: the tax office's rule
realWorld.text: Singapore's tax authority, IRAS, tells companies: "Your company must retain its records for at least 5 years from the relevant YA." YA is the year of assessment, the tax year for the income. Fenwhistle's 7 years for invoices covers that, as given data in this story; your own duty depends on where you trade.

realWorld.title: The same question for AI: LATENT, Who Owns the Answer
realWorld.text: LATENT's Who Owns the Answer builds on this case.

asked: How do you design a system so data can really be deleted?
How would you answer a data access request?
What does data minimisation change in a schema?
interview.answer: Start from purpose. For every kind of personal data, write down why it is collected, how long it is kept and why, and who owns that decision; that is the retention schedule. Then design for deletion from the first table. Every record carries its kind and the case or account it serves, so a job can find what has expired. The deletion job runs on a fixed day, writes a list of what it deleted by id, never by contents, and skips anything an open request or a legal duty to keep it covers. Backups are where deletion usually fails, so keep them on a fixed cycle, say 35 days, and say plainly that deleted data leaves the last copy by then; after any restore, run the deletion list again. Copies outside the main store, exports, emails, reporting copies, need the same labels or they escape. For an access request: verify identity, search every store you control, hold those records while you answer, take third parties out by masking or leaving them out, and send within the deadline: where GDPR applies, one month, extendable by two for complex requests; where the PDPA applies, the PDPC's guidance says as soon as reasonably possible and a written note if you can't within 30 days. Minimisation changes the schema itself, the layout of a database's tables and columns: fewer columns, coarser values where coarse is enough, such as a month rather than a birth date, and no free-text field that invites notes on people who aren't your customers. I'd close with the investigator's story: an agency that kept everything turned a routine request into three strangers' evenings from 2016; with a schedule, labels and a 35-day backup cycle, that file would have left the drive and every backup years before anyone asked.

terms.def: The four-person private-investigation agency in Singapore in this story, founded by Mr Thiruchelvam in 2014. Vasanthi is its night researcher.

What the investigators wrote down while working a client's case: what was asked, what they did, what they found. Five per case.
Records about people a case touched who never hired the agency, such as neighbours seen from the street. Two per case; 428 in all.
A bill sent to a client. Tax rules usually say how long invoices must be kept.
Anything that can identify a living person, such as a name, a phone number or a note of when someone leaves home.
A person asking an organisation for a copy of the personal data it holds about them. In many places the organisation must answer within a set time.
Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act 2012. Among its obligations: access to personal data, protecting it, and retention limitation.
Singapore's Personal Data Protection Commission, which enforces the PDPA and publishes guidance and decisions.
The EU's General Data Protection Regulation. Article 5 sets purpose limitation, data minimisation and storage limitation; Article 15 gives the right to a copy.
The office computer's store of all the agency's files, which everyone in the office works from. Here, the live data.
The working copy of the records, the one people open every day, as opposed to the backups.
A spare copy of data kept somewhere else, to restore from after a mistake. Fenwhistle copies its whole drive every night at 02:00.
Copying a backup back into the live data. Restoring an old copy also brings back anything deleted since that copy was made.
How long each backup copy is kept before it is deleted, such as 35 days. Data deleted from the live store leaves the last copy one cycle later.
Scrambling data with a key so only someone holding the key can read it. It keeps outsiders out; it does not decide what is kept.
The reason a piece of personal data was collected, such as a car case in November 2016. When the purpose ends, so does the reason to keep it.
Data collected for one reason is used for that reason, and not for new ones the person was never told about.
Collecting and keeping only what the purpose needs. GDPR: adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary.
GDPR's rule that data which identifies people is kept no longer than its purpose needs. The PDPA's version is the retention limitation obligation.
PDPA section 25: stop keeping personal data, or make it anonymous, once its purpose is no longer served and no legal or business purpose needs it.
A written list of each kind of record, how long it is kept, and why. Fenwhistle's: 7 years for most kinds, 1 year for notes on others, as given data.
A tag on each record saying its kind and the case it serves, so a deletion job can tell kinds apart and apply each its own keep period.
A job that deletes every record past its keep period on a fixed day. Fenwhistle's first is on Monday 26 October 2026.
Anyone named in a file who is not the person asking, such as Ms Brannigan's three neighbours. Their data is taken out of her reply.
Hiding other people's personal data in a document before handing it over, such as blacking out a name. The PDPC suggests it for access replies.
Agreement a person gives freely to the use of their own data for purposes they were told about. It covers that person only.
Removing whatever links data to particular people, so it no longer identifies anyone. The PDPA treats this as a way to stop retaining it.
The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore, its tax authority. It asks companies to keep records for at least 5 years from the relevant year of assessment.
IRAS's name for the tax year in which income is assessed: income earned in one year is assessed in the next.
An international standard for running information security. Annex A control A.5.34 covers privacy and protection of personally identifiable information, and A.8.10 information deletion.

An audit report, written by an outside checker, on a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. Its optional privacy criteria cover retaining and disposing of personal information.
The Data Protection Trustmark, a Singapore certification that an organisation's personal data practices meet a published standard.

atWork: Look for the table, bucket or folder kept "just in case" with no deletion date. It is a common pattern: an old exports folder, an analytics table nobody owns, a support tool that keeps every transcript, logs with customers' names in them. For each, ask four things. What is it for, and is that purpose still served? How long is it kept, and where is the reason written down? Does each record carry enough of a label (its kind, its customer, its date) for a job to find what has expired? And when it is deleted, when does it leave the last backup? Then build a retention schedule, a deletion job that skips anything an open request covers, a backup cycle with a known length (on AWS, for example, a lifecycle rule on an S3 bucket or a retention period on AWS Backup), and a written way to answer access requests that takes third parties out. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, this is Annex A 5.34 (privacy and protection of personally identifiable information) and A.8.10 (information deletion); if it operates in Singapore and is covered by the PDPA, it is the retention limitation and access obligations, and the Data Protection Trustmark (DPTM) assesses the same practices; if you hold EU residents' data, GDPR Articles 5 and 15 may apply; and if your SOC 2 report includes the privacy category, its criteria on retaining and disposing of personal information apply. A store with no retention rule is a finding an auditor is likely to raise, and backups with no fixed cycle are the part teams most often have to rebuild, so set both in the first design rather than at audit time. None of this is legal advice: check your own duties with someone qualified.

recall.prompt: Your company's support app keeps every chat transcript forever, in its main database and in nightly backups that are never deleted. A former customer asks for all the data you hold about her. Her transcripts also mention other customers by name. What do you send her, and what would you change in the system?

keyIdeas.idea: Answer within the deadline with her own data, taking third parties out by masking or leaving them out
Set a retention schedule: a purpose and a keep period per kind of data, then delete on time
Make deletion reach the backups with a fixed backup cycle

recall.model: Send her a copy of her own personal data within the time allowed, after checking it is really her, with the other customers' names taken out by masking or leaving them out: third parties' data is not hers to receive. Then fix the system. Write a retention schedule: for each kind of data, its purpose, a keep period and the reason, such as transcripts kept while a complaint could still come back and then deleted. Label each record so a deletion job can find what has expired, run it on a fixed day, and have it skip anything an open request covers. Finally, give the backups a fixed cycle, such as 35 days, so deleted data ages out of the backup copies by a date you can name, and run the deletion list again after any restore.

recall.prompt: Fenwhistle encrypts its shared drive and its backups but keeps every record. What changes in Ms Brannigan's reply?
options: Nothing: it still holds her 2016 file and names 3 neighbours
It names no neighbours, because their notes are scrambled
It is empty, because encrypted files can't be searched
It holds only her contact details
recall.why: The agency holds the key, so its own search reads every record as before. Encryption changes what a thief sees, not what the agency keeps or hands over.

recall.prompt: Which GDPR principle says data that identifies people should be kept no longer than its purpose needs?
recall.why: Storage limitation, Article 5(1)(e): kept in a form which permits identification for no longer than is necessary for the purposes. Minimisation is about how much is collected.

recall.prompt: Fenwhistle deletes the 2016 file from its drive on Monday 26 October 2026, and keeps each nightly backup copy 35 days. When is the file gone from every backup?
recall.why: The last copy made before the deletion is deleted 35 days later: 26 October plus 35 days is Monday 30 November 2026.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Since its first run on 26 October, the schedule has run on the first Monday of each month, and every backup copy lives 35 days. On Monday 4 January 2027, the first run of the new year, it deleted 184 records: the contact details, case notes and invoices of 2019's 18 cases, and the notes on other people from 2025's 20 cases. On Thursday 7 January the shared drive's disk failed. Mr Thiruchelvam restored the drive from the nightly copy of Sunday 3 January, and we were working again by morning. Tonight I searched for a 2019 client's name for a routine check. Her file was back.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why are the 184 deleted records back on the drive, and what should change so a restore can't undo a deletion?

keyIdeas.idea: The copy restored was made before the 4 January deletion run, so it still held those records
Keep a list of deleted record ids (not contents) and run it again after every restore
Make the check part of the restore steps: after any restore, confirm nothing past its keep period came back

coldCase.model: The deletion worked; the restore undid it. The copy from Sunday 3 January was made before the run on Monday 4 January, so it still held the 184 records, and restoring it put them back on the drive. A backup cycle only removes deleted data from copies made after the deletion. Keep a deletion list: every run writes down the ids of what it deleted, never the contents. Make running it again part of the restore steps, so after any restore the job removes anything on the list, and then checks that nothing past its keep period came back. The same list answers a regulator who asks what was deleted and when.
